entries.english: Maternal uncle (mother's brother; Krapf & Rebmann 1887, p. 9)
entries.translation: maternal uncle (mother's brother; Krapf & Rebmann 1887, p. 9)
entries.context: In traditional Mijikenda matrilineal (fugo / lukolo) kinship, the maternal uncle (avu) exercised authority over his sister's children (muhua, pl. ahua).

entries.english: Nephew or niece (a man's sister's son or daughter; Krapf & Rebmann 1887, p. 276)
entries.translation: nephew or niece (a man's sister's son or daughter; Krapf & Rebmann 1887, p. 276)
entries.context: Hiyu ni muhua wangu, muana wa mumbuyangu (This is my nephew/niece, my sister's child).

entries.english: Welcome! (traditional Mijikenda greeting of hospitality; Krapf & Rebmann 1887, p. 390)
entries.translation: welcome! (traditional Mijikenda greeting of hospitality; Krapf & Rebmann 1887, p. 390)
entries.context: Yoyo, mugeni! Yoyo mulumangu! udzihenda to kudza na afia. Yoyo baba! Yoyo nduguyangu!

entries.english: Communal rain-making charm and three-day ritual restriction (Krapf & Rebmann 1887, p. 352)
entries.translation: communal rain-making charm and three-day ritual restriction (Krapf & Rebmann 1887, p. 352)
entries.context: Villagers gather food for two days because on the third day (muhondo) no one may go to the fields; they drag a skin (kichingo) and perform the sosonga rain rite.

entries.english: Traditional Rabai spicy condiment/vinegar (Krapf & Rebmann 1887, p. 346)
entries.translation: traditional Rabai spicy condiment/vinegar (Krapf & Rebmann 1887, p. 346)
entries.context: Pounded from sorghum flour (unga wa muhama), red pepper (pilipili), kilungakuku herb, palm-wine dregs (muniu zira za uchi), and lemon (ndimu) or makabu fruit.

source: Public Domain Historical Lexicons (Krapf 1850, Krapf & Rebmann 1887, W. E. Taylor 1891 & Johnston 1919)
